newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Feb CPI rises 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Feb CPI rises 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.3 percent in February after a 0.1 percent advance in January. Minus food and energy items, the so-called "core" CPI rose 0.2 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2 percent rise in both the overall and core rates.
CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AND CO INC: "Slightly worse than expected ... (but) all in all, today's number I don't think would make the (Federal Reserve) tighten."
Katz was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

DOUGLAS PORTER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NESBITT BURNS SECURITIES INC, TORONTO: "It isn't a friendly number, but not as bad as first glance. It is a bit of a surprise on the high side given the exceptional PPI report (on Friday). We are still seeing a bit of a hangover from the high energy prices from late last year and early this year, but that will be reversed big time in the months ahead.
"I don't think it will be a negative for the (bond) market. The core rate is still only up 2.5 year over year."

DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS: "I thought energy prices were on their way down, but they were up. Food prices were up. When (Fed chief Alan) Greenspan mentions the CPI, he always talks about the core, and that's up only two tenths.
"It's still very modest. Year-to-date you're running at 2.2 percent on the core versus 2.6 for all of last year.
"I don't think this really sways the Fed one way or the other. I don't think this provides inflation ammunition for the Fed to tighten. They have economic ammunition, but not inflation ammunition."
Sloan went on: "Overall, the report is just marginally disappointing. It doesn't change the big picture. We think the Federal Reserve is likely to tighten at its next meeting."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "CPI is in trend performance...the headline actually reflects what's going on within the components. It was a potential swing-factor for the Fed. If you had a high CPI, that gives them political cover to go ahead and raise rates. If it was subdued, then it kind of postpones the reaction. What we're seeing is right in the middle."

JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES CORP: "It was a disappointment and the disapointment goes beyond just the energy component. I felt energy would be down 0.1 percent and most people were looking for bigger declines than that. If it wasn't for the second consecutive large drop in transportation ... the core would have been up 0.3 percent.

"It's not a troublesome surge in inflation, but I don't think the Fed really needs anything much more than what they're seeing right now in terms of the on-the-ground inflation, given how strong the real side of the economy has been, is now and looks like it will be," Liro said.

MICHAEL P. NIEMIRA, ECONOMIST, BANK OF TOKYO-MITSUBISHI LTD: "The story line doesn't seem to be anything different than what we've seen all along and we're still locked in a narrow range for CPI. The thing that caught my eye is transportation is down, that may reverse in next month's report, but it's more specific price changes as opposed to the broader inflationary concern.

"It's a neutral (for the Fed). I don't think it sways them one way or another. All it says is we haven't seen any breakout in terms of inflationary pressures and that's not news to them. I still suspect the Fed will move rates higher."

ROBERT DEDERICK, CHIEF-ECONOMIST, NORTHERN TRUST: "(The numbers) are non-threatening. They're good, but not so good that Alan Greenspan can relax his guard. The safest forecasts on the Fed (for March) is a 50/50 percent chance (of a tightening of monetary policy), but I have leaned to 60/40 that they will tighten."

Commenting on the specific parts of the data, Dederick said: "Both food and energy were up just a tad. There wasn't anything really here -- at least on the surfice -- that seems to have been terribly out of line."
